title: Extinction strain rate: where does the flame go out?
summary: Strain rate at which a counterflow flame extinguishes, plotted against equivalence ratio on a log axis, with competing models and measured points. It tests how robust the chemistry is, not just how fast the flame burns.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of extinction strain rate against equivalence ratio with two model curves and orange experiment markers with error bars.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Where does the flame extinguish?
read_the_figure.axes: x: equivalence ratio phi (dimensionless). y: extinction strain rate a_ext in 1/s on a logarithmic scale.
look_at: Do the markers sit on model A, model B, or between?
How steep is each curve? A straight line on a log axis means exponential growth with phi.
Where is the vertical gap between models largest (a ratio, not a difference)?
What are the flame conditions: temperature, pressure, fuel?
read_the_figure.proves: A model whose extinction curve passes through the markers captures the balance between chemical heat release and flow-driven loss, which is a harder test than flame speed. It tests the chemistry near extinction, where radical recombination dominates.
if_wrong: A model curve that is parallel to the data but shifted: a constant factor error in the controlling chemistry.
Two models that agree on flame speed but differ here: flame speed alone cannot rank them.
Missing conditions (burner geometry, nozzle separation, Tu, p): strain rates are not comparable between rigs.

terms.meaning: Rate of stretching of the flow normal to the flame front, in 1/s. For opposed jets it is velocity over separation, up to a geometry factor.
The strain rate at which the flame can no longer sustain itself and goes out as strain is raised in small steps.
Two opposed nozzles, one fuel, one oxidiser or premixed gas; a flat flame sits between them and strain is set by the flow.
y logarithmic. Equal distances are equal ratios.

remember: Extinction strain is the flame's resistance to being stretched apart: larger means stronger flame.
On this plot a straight line is exponential growth: ln a_ext = ln a_0 + b phi.
Compare models by vertical ratios, not differences.
Always give the geometry: nozzle separation, unburned temperature, pressure.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along x encodes phi, position along y the logarithm of extinction strain. Line style and colour separate the models (solid and dashed), and orange filled circles with error bars are measurements. The annotation points to one marker to say what the y value means: above it the flame is out.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Extinction strain varies over more than an order of magnitude as the mixture becomes richer, so a log axis keeps every point visible. The strain a flame survives depends on how fast the heat release can compensate loss by stretch; fast radical chemistry gives high values. Models with equal flame speed can differ in a_ext, so the plot is an independent test.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Which model is closer to the data? Model A (solid teal) passes through or within the error bars of all seven markers, while model B (dashed blue) lies above them for phi below 0.8. Q2: How much does extinction strain change from phi = 0.4 to 1.0 in the data? The marker rises from about 8e2 to 9e3 1/s: a factor of roughly 11, so a_ext grows by a factor of 1.5 for every 0.1 step in phi (e^0.4). Q3: Where do the models differ most? At the lean end, phi = 0.4, model B is about 1.4e3 against 8e2 for model A, a ratio of about 1.7; at phi = 1.0 they agree.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Data markers: the figure overlays the experimental points with error bars; without them the two models would only be compared with one another, and the plot would say which model is different, not which is right.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Log axes shrink ratios: a model off by a factor 1.7 at phi = 0.4 looks like a modest vertical gap. Strain rate is not a unique number: its definition (a local or a global definition from the nozzle) changes the value by tens of percent, so the markers carry a hidden definition. Points that vary smoothly can hide a gap between steady and unsteady extinction.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the ratio model over experiment against phi to show the error directly. For physical insight use the S-shaped curve of peak temperature against strain rate, whose turning point is extinction. A table of a_ext gives exact numbers.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a lower panel with the ratio model over experiment and a band for experimental uncertainty, or add a third axis showing the characteristic flow time 1/a_ext in microseconds.

steps.title: Strain rate between opposed jets
steps.note: Seshadri-Williams form for opposed-jet nozzles; the factor changes with nozzle design, so say which definition is used.

steps.title: An exponential trend read as a line on log y
steps.note: The slope on the semi-log plot is the growth rate b.

worked.title: Growth rate of extinction strain from model A
worked.problem: Model A passes through a_ext = 9000 1/s at phi = 1.0 and 816 1/s at phi = 0.4. Find b, and the factor per 0.1 step.

solution.text: Slope of ln a against phi.

worked.answer: b = 4.0 per unit phi, so a_ext rises 49 percent per 0.1 increase in phi.

analyze.hint: Which part of the chemistry matters near extinction?
